I may get downvoted but I've always thought that, while on one level an extraordinary film that part of me still can't quite believe ever got greenlit on that budget, Fight Club is ultimately a bit silly and adolescent. It's very "young Fincher"/Gen X in tone, which is fine I guess but as someone who was a teenager back then I feel like I've very much moved on.

That said it's an extraordinary achievement technically as much as anything, and a small part of me does still find it pretty damn cool. Like, it's very much of its time and place, but it was a cool time and place I guess.

I think that Fight Club is an extraordinarily insightful critique of not just toxic masculinity, but also the culture that produces toxic masculinity. That it is very easy for people to misinterpret is not the movie’s fault, but rather a testament to its complexity.

On my most recent rewatch, I developed a theory that the movie is about the narrator struggling with his gender identity, and that not only is Tyler Durden a creation of his subconscious, but so are Marla Singer and Bob. They represent the battle between his internal feminine and masculine sides, with Bob as a personified warped outcome of that battle (he has breasts, but only because he was injecting himself with testosterone, so his body rebelled against the outside of influence of excessive masculinity by developing more feminine physical traits).

It was my favorite film and inteoduced me to Chuck Palahniuk, who was my favorite writer when I was a teenager. I probably watched the movie 20 times.

And 2-3 years ago, in my 30s I watched it again. I feel the same way as you. I think the concept is very teenage angst. However, maybe the vook and the movie was trying to show that in a satirical way? Like we were supposed to see the teenage side of it when we watched? I was rolling my eyes at every Tyler Durden quote

I like it but I’m also not surprised some people miss the point because the film often feels just as in love with Tyler as they are. I sometimes wish it didn’t have the half-hearted “actually everything you’ve just seen is bad” denouement of the last half hour and just went all-out until the end, as satire it would feel more biting.

I think that's because the messages are very poigniant, if ironically misunderstood for teenage men. 

As you get older, the message becomes more and more absurdist, because it is lol.

It still remains my favorite movie because it completely reshaped my worldview, or more accurately, opened my brain to a worldview because I didn't have much of one to begin with until I watched this movie.
Whether or not Marla and Bob are real, that's a really great theory/interpretation on what they represent.

This is my problem with the film. It does the seduction of the Fight Club idea and Tyler Durden a bit TOO well, which is why everyone who is a young male especially falls under the spell and says "Hey I want that", even though it's a pretty destructive idea.

Here is where I'll say the book is better at that front in some ways...it actually highlights some moments where Tyler Durden is not cool and gets stuff wrong (Especially the finale)

Yeah it’s definitely a satire, unfortunately a lot of people who watched the movie missed the point and are on Durden’s side

For me, it's always been a good movie driven by healthy, yet sufficiently cynical, youthful rebellion, stylistic brio and truly iconic moments - in the true sense that they entered popular culture beyond the film itself. Much like the unintentionally hilariously po-faced, yet equally influential, Matrix from the same year, it acted as fin de siecle capstone to the Prada-Meinhoff 90s and ushered in the more unashamedly capitalist and tech-infused 00s.

However, the people who took it far too seriously back then are as bad as the people who like to use mocking it as a launchpad for their supposed intellectual superiority today.

It's a pop-theory Hollywood movie, not a blueprint for a personality. I mean, it explicitly told us not to talk about it...

I think humans in general, regardless of gender or age, have a slight tendency to be self-destructive. Alcohol, smoking, etc. There's something about doing something that hurts us that just attracts some people.

Exactly, it was my favorite movie for years because there are so many ways to appreciate it. It's so solidly made and has a ton of style and so many ideas and easter eggs, and it actually has a ton to say about America's newest "lost generation" and dips into the "God is dead" existentialism and all that. It's also heavy handed about all of it yet it works because it's written so well and (in the movie) Pitt is perfect. Another thing, kind of a side note, is how it highlights what "wokeism" used to be, more of an inclusive, underground, subcultural sort of collectivist-oriented mindset than something anchored so heavily on identity politics and individualism.
If durden was speaking nonsense the character wouldn’t work. His platitudes connect to a very real part of the feelings of young men in America. It’s immaturity is it’s honesty.

My recollection is hazy, but here's what I remember:

There's a guy, the narrator, who is a wiener. He leads a normal life, follows the rules, and feels like a sad loser.

He meets Tyler Durden who seems to be one of those people who sees the system for the illusion it is and is somehow able to do everything you're not supposed to do and win.

A big thread of this is about the neutering of masculinity in modern life. The narrator is a neutered man, and Tyler is a manly man.

So they start a fight club where men can remember what it is to be men through violence!

The Fight Club becomes a cult and then a terrorist organization, but it only really goes sideways when Tyler targets Marla. And that's when the narrator throws off the yoke of civilization ending macho fascism and rescues the babe by shooting himself in the head.

The thing that is missing from the arc, to me, is that the narrator never seems to me to develop a sense of self esteem. There's no epiphany about how to live that isn't being a macho bad ass who burns the world down. 

I think disaffected men joining a violent fascist cult definitely still resonates today. But, Fight Club's answer of "If you want the girl you have to leave the macho woman hating cult" isn't the answer. Because a lot of the time an inability to get the girl in the first place is one of the causes of the disaffection that funnels young men into fascism.

I always thought the silly, adolescent aspect is intentional—I mean, the men’s right angle is satire, epitomized by cutting the big dong into children’s cinema, right?

That’s still makes me laugh—the seriousness & solemnity the characters treat that act has got to be satire
It is a satire but I saw another kind when I rewatched. Not what it intended and people perceived in the late 90s early 2000s

It seems a little silly to keep blaming the audience for this reading when it is one of, if not the predominant reading of the film. 

If you don’t like this reading (which I do not), it seems a lot more appropriate to blame Fincher and Uhls for making a anti-hypermasculine work that can easily be read as the opposite. 

The fact is, there is no meaningful repudiation to Tyler’s ideology and behavior in the film. The fact that the book has a much different end means there is no running away from the fact that the Uhls screenplay softened the ending significantly and allows a much more positive reading of the actions of Tyler and the Narrator.

Granted, you definitely have to be immature, an asshole, or both to look at the way Tyler and the Narrator treat the people around them as anything but terrible. But it turns out there’s a lot of immature assholes out there and those traits correlate strongly with men that cling to traditional masculinity. 

Anyway, I don’t think it’s unfair to say Fincher is excellent at many aspects of filmmaking, but he very much struggles with sticking the landing on endings. The Killer’s ending is also atrocious and I think it will be remembered in a similar way once all the masturbatory praise of the technical skills has a few years to get old.

>Gen X in tone

That right there is the part where I think people get lost and lose sight of a lot of the point the movie is trying to make. There's so much Gen X aggravation in Fight Club. A great example is the line about "Our fathers were our model for God, if our fathers bail what does that tell us about God". Children of divorce made up a higher percentage of Gen Xers than other generations. 

There so much stuff in there like that. An angry generation coming out of the shallow materialism of the 80s.

What the toxic masculinity interpretation misses is that there are some aspects of Tyler Durden that the narrator (the last man) is supposed  to take on. You're  just not supposed  to take all of them on 100%. It's a Nietzschean metamorphosis. http://nietzsche.holtof.com/Nietzsche_thus_spake_zarathustra/I_01.html

Well yes, it’s intended ironically. And yet…is it, 100%? Whose side is Fincher actually on? I can’t help but think he kind of admires Tyler. Or at the very least he seems super creatively inspired by him.

I have a similar problem with some Scorsese movies. Like, ok those gangsters sure get their comeuppance and yeah, I don’t for a second think Scorsese himself would feel anything other than disgusted by them irl. But goddamn if the movies themselves aren’t massively in love with them.

I’m not trying to sound smug, but I absolutely never fell for it even as a teenager, as some sort of lifestyle or something. What I found cool was the sheer filmmaking verve and what I saw as an incredibly smart critique of capitalism (I probably didn’t latch onto the masculinity stuff so much when younger, probably because I was less aware of that as an issue).

Now I just think it’s a bit shallow and “clever clever”. Like, very much including the layers of irony. It’s smart but it’s not deep, whereas personally I think with Se7en, say, even the early Fincher found a profundity that completely eluded him in Fight Club. Obviously his later stuff is another story again.

Sure—that’s kinda the brilliance, though, right?

Men’s Rights, pick up artists, bro-culture, etc., has a lot of toxicity—but stripped of those labels, there’s also a lot that has undeniable appeal to most young men …

It’s not like cult members start out to join a cult. 

There’s a rhetorical principle called the enthymeme, wherein you start from a common premise then escalate

*None of us want to be bullied, right?*

*Aren’t you tired of women having all the power in sexual relationships?*

*Working 9 to 5 is just a racket, yeah?*

Once you get buy in on any number of fairly benign concepts, which are often unspoken because of social norms, you steadily climb a logic chain.

Inside the bubble, the conclusions seem obvious—from the outside, they seem radical, or insane.

*Fight Club* pretty much takes us on that journey, while winking at us the all along the way—I mean, Tyler is hard to not like, as he sweeps us forward to increasingly radical actions.

I thought the insomnia/lack of sleep was a bit of a tell, representing the vulnerability of ‘normal’ people living our lives of quiet desperation.

I dunno—that was kind of my take. There’s a lot of different levels working in *Fight Club*, which is why I thought it was pretty brilliant.
